book_title: Hymn to the Nile (Praise to Hapi)
author: Middle Kingdom Egyptian Scribe Tradition (c. 2100 BC)
provenance_note: Public-domain English verse rendering of the Middle Kingdom Egyptian 'Hymn to Hapi' (the spirit of the annual Nile flood), preserved on apprentice scribes' papyrus rolls including Papyrus Sallier II in the British Museum.
author_context: Without rain in the scorching Sahara Desert, all of Ancient Egypt depended on one giant river bursting its banks every July. Read this 4,000-year-old hymn aloud to hear how villagers celebrated the rising water.
cover_caption: Painted tomb wall from Thebes showing a barefoot Egyptian gardener pulling a wooden shaduf rope beside lush pomegranate trees and his little dog.

vocabVault.def: The life-giving summer flood when the River Nile burst its banks and spread rich black mud over the fields.
Ancient Egypt's name for itself, meaning 'Black Land', after the dark fertile river silt left behind by floods.
Tall marsh reeds growing along the Nile that Egyptians pressed into smooth writing sheets and plaited into sandals.
Fine, nutrient-rich dark river mud carried downstream by floodwater to help wheat and barley grow.

extract:
Every summer across dry Egypt, families watched the southern sky and waited eagerly for the river to rise. Four thousand years ago, Egyptian pupils copied a joyful song onto papyrus rolls to thank the annual Nile inundation.
Hail to you, O Nile, rising out of the earth,
Coming in peace to keep all Egypt alive!
You water the green orchards created by Ra,
And give cool drink to every thirsty flock.
When your flood delays, every breath grows weak,
And rich and poor cry out together in fear!
Yet when you rise, the Black Land shouts for joy,
Every belly is glad and every back shakes with laughter!
You bring sweet bread and fill the storehouses wide,
Remembering the poor family waiting at the gate.
Sweet harps ring out to praise your dark mud,
And children clap their hands along the river bank!
Without that yearly gift of black silt, golden wheat could never sprout beside scorching desert sand.

parent_discussion.question: In the first verse of the hymn, what happened across Egypt whenever the Nile flood was late?
parent_discussion.answer: Every breath grew weak, and rich and poor people cried out together in fear because the orchards and flocks needed the rising water.

parent_discussion.question: Why does the poet say 'every belly is glad and every back shakes with laughter' as soon as the floodwaters rise?
parent_discussion.answer: Rising waters left behind damp black Kemet mud, guaranteeing full grain storehouses, fresh bread, and relief for every family.

parent_discussion.question: Usually people are frightened when a river floods—why did Egyptian children clap their hands and adults play harps to welcome this flood?
parent_discussion.answer: In dry desert Egypt, the yearly flood brought cool drinking water and rich black silt so golden wheat could grow, filling storehouses with sweet bread for rich and poor alike.

story_check.question: What happened when the Nile flood rose on time in the second verse?
options: Families fled permanently into the dry mountains
The Black Land shouted for joy and storehouses filled with food
Farmers stopped planting wheat and barley altogether
Priests banned harp music beside the river
story_check.feedback: Spot on! The hymn celebrates how the rising flood brought dark mud, full storehouses, harp music, and laughter across Kemet.

story_check.question: Who suffered if the Nile inundation failed to arrive?
options: Only foreign sea merchants
Only camel drivers in the eastern hills
Both rich people and poor families alike
Nobody, because heavy rain fell every week in Egypt
story_check.feedback: Correct! Across dry Egypt, both rich and poor cried out together in fear whenever the flood was late.

story_check.question: What left the soil along the Nile banks dark and rich enough to grow wheat and barley?
options: Black volcanic ash blown from Italy
Crushed charcoal spread by soldiers
Rich black silt carried downstream by summer floodwaters
Salty seawater washing inland from the sea
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! The yearly flood washed rich black silt downstream onto Egypt's fields so wheat and barley could grow.

monday_cold_call.question: In the Ancient Egyptian 'Hymn to the Nile', why did children clap and adults laugh when dark muddy floodwater covered their fields?
monday_cold_call.answer: Because the sinking flood left behind rich black silt (Kemet) needed to grow wheat and barley for bread across the desert kingdom.

hinge_question: Why did Ancient Egyptians sing hymns of praise to a flooding river when floods in many other countries are feared as disasters?

book_title: Garlic, Bread and Wet Sand at Giza
author: The History Revision Hub Narrative Archive
provenance_note: Original historical micro-story grounded in the 2013 Wadi al-Jarf papyrus logbooks of Inspector Merer (c. 2560 BC) and Dr Mark Lehner's archaeological excavations of the Heit el-Ghurab pyramid-builders' village at Giza.
author_context: For centuries, people guessed that whipped slaves built the Great Pyramid of Giza. Then archaeologists dug up the builders' real town and even found Boat Inspector Merer's 4,500-year-old papyrus diary!
cover_caption: Sunlit stone house walls and neat narrow streets inside an Ancient Egyptian royal tomb-builders' village nestled below desert cliffs.

vocabVault.def: The rocky desert plateau near modern Cairo where Pharaoh Khufu raised the 146-metre Great Pyramid.
Fine, gleaming white stone quarried across the Nile and floated by barge to case the outside of Khufu's pyramid.
A heavy wooden frame on smooth runners pulled with ropes over wet desert sand to move two-tonne stone blocks.
Studying human history by digging up and examining buildings, bones, tools, and food remains left underground.

extract: Dawn broke pink over Giza around 2560 BC. Warm woodsmoke drifted from rows of dome-shaped mud ovens. Inside the walled builders' village, bakers tipped hot loaves of fresh bread out of clay moulds. Nobody stood cracking whips over starving slaves here. Down at the canal harbour, Boat Inspector Merer opened his papyrus logbook and dipped his reed pen in ink. His forty-man crew had just floated shining white limestone blocks across the flooded Nile from Tura quarry. Proud teams painted bold gang names onto blocks, calling themselves "Friends of Khufu" and "Drunkards of Menkaure". Out on the ramp, a young worker sloshed river water onto the sand ahead of a wooden sledge. Wet sand halved rubbing friction! Haulers pulled the two-tonne stone steadily skyward. At sunset, tired crews shared roasted Nile fish, beef, sweet onions, and crisp garlic. Four thousand years later, ash-filled bakeries and healed bones proved well-fed Egyptian teams built the Great Pyramid.

parent_discussion.question: What clever trick did Giza workers use to stop heavy wooden sledges from digging into dry desert sand?
parent_discussion.answer: A worker poured river water onto the sand right in front of the sledge runners, halving friction so blocks slid smoothly.

parent_discussion.question: What do team names like 'Friends of Khufu' tell us about how the pyramid builders felt about their work?
parent_discussion.answer: They worked in proud teams who enjoyed naming their gangs and took pride in building for Pharaoh Khufu, rather than being whipped, starving slaves.

parent_discussion.question: Many people used to think starving, whipped slaves built the Great Pyramid—what details in this story would surprise them most?
parent_discussion.answer: The builders lived in a walled village with fresh bread ovens, ate roasted fish, beef, onions, and garlic, gave themselves proud team names, and left behind healed bones and ash-filled bakeries.

story_check.question: What was Boat Inspector Merer's job in the story at Giza?
options: A Roman general attacking Alexandria
An Egyptian boat inspector floating white Tura limestone to Giza
A Greek poet writing stories about monsters
A tomb robber hiding gold inside a cave
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Inspector Merer wrote in his papyrus logbook as his forty-man crew floated shining white limestone blocks from Tura quarry to Giza.

story_check.question: Why did a worker pour water onto the sand in front of each wooden sledge?
options: To grow wheat right on top of the pyramid ramp
To wash away painted hieroglyphs on the stones
To dampen the sand and halve friction under the heavy runners
To cool down bronze chariot wheels
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Dampening dry sand bound the grains together and cut sliding friction in half.

story_check.question: Which clues proved four thousand years later that well-fed Egyptian teams built the Great Pyramid?
options: Iron railway tracks and steam cranes
Ash-filled bread bakeries and healed bones
Stacks of printed paper banknotes
Marble theatres seating ten thousand people
story_check.feedback: Well remembered! Ash-filled bakeries and healed bones proved that Giza's builders were well-fed, cared-for teams.

monday_cold_call.question: What clues in our Giza story show that well-fed Egyptian teams—not whipped slaves—built the Great Pyramid?
monday_cold_call.answer: Ash-filled bread bakeries, healed bones, proud gang names like 'Friends of Khufu', and Inspector Merer's boat logbook.

hinge_question: Why is a rubbish heap of ancient fish bones and bakery ash outside Giza just as exciting to a historian as a golden crown?

book_title: The Instruction of Dua-Kheti (The Satire of the Trades)
author: Dua-Kheti (Middle Kingdom Egypt, c. 1900 BC)
provenance_note: Public-domain English verse adaptation of 'The Instruction of Dua-Kheti' (popularly called 'The Satire of the Trades'), Egypt's most copied Middle and New Kingdom school text, preserved on Papyrus Sallier II and hundreds of limestone ostraca.
author_context: Almost four thousand years ago, an Egyptian father named Dua-Kheti sailed south up the Nile to drop his young son Pepi at scribe school. Listen to the funny warnings he gave Pepi to make him practise his 700 hieroglyphs!
cover_caption: Pressed golden-brown Egyptian papyrus scroll covered in crisp columns of black and red ink written with a reed brush.

vocabVault.def: A respected Ancient Egyptian official trained for years to read and write hieroglyphs, count taxes, and keep royal records.
Ancient Egypt's sacred writing system combining over 700 picture signs and sound symbols.
Clever, funny writing that exaggerates everyday problems to make readers laugh and think.
Broken pottery shards or flat limestone flakes used like cheap scrap notebooks by trainee scribes.

extract:
Nearly four thousand years ago, an Egyptian father named Dua-Kheti sailed south up the Nile with his young son Pepi. Pepi was starting at the royal school for scribes, so his father recited a witty poem to stop him daydreaming.
Set your whole heart on books, my son,
For nothing beats learning how to write!
I have watched the smith beside his roaring furnace,
With fingers wrinkled like rough crocodile skin.
The reed-cutter toils until his bare arms ache,
While hungry mosquitoes bite his face at dusk!
The potter kneels smeared in wet river clay,
Dirtier than pigs snuffling round the yard.
The cobbler chews tough leather strips all day,
And the washerman scrubs beside lurking crocodiles!
Look round: no job on Earth escapes a boss,
Except the scribe—for he gives out the orders!
Trainee scribes laughed at Kheti's jokes for centuries, copying his verses onto pottery scraps until their reed brushes flew neatly across papyrus.

parent_discussion.question: Which unpleasant dangers or discomforts does Dua-Kheti describe for the smith, the reed-cutter, and the washerman?
parent_discussion.answer: The smith gets fingers rough as crocodile skin by his hot furnace, mosquitoes bite the reed-cutter, and crocodiles lurk near the washerman.

parent_discussion.question: Do you think Dua-Kheti was being completely fair to Egypt's skilled potters and cobblers, or exaggerating on purpose?
parent_discussion.answer: He was exaggerating on purpose for a laugh! Like all satire, he made other jobs sound messy and dangerous so his son Pepi would focus on learning to write.

parent_discussion.question: If you were young Pepi listening to your dad's funny poem on the boat, would it persuade you to work hard at scribe school? Why?
parent_discussion.answer: Learning over 700 hieroglyphs took years of practice, yet becoming a scribe meant counting taxes, keeping royal records, and giving out orders instead of dodging crocodiles or chewing leather!

story_check.question: Where was Dua-Kheti taking his young son Pepi as they sailed up the River Nile?
options: To fight chariots in Syria
To enrol him at the royal school for scribes
To hunt hippos in the northern delta
To quarry granite stones at Aswan
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Kheti was taking Pepi to scribe school and wanted him to work hard at his lessons.

story_check.question: What does Dua-Kheti compare the smith's wrinkled fingers to in his poem?
options: Smooth Nile lotus petals
Rough crocodile skin
Soft white linen cloth
Polished gold rings
story_check.feedback: Haha, yes! That funny line—'fingers wrinkled like rough crocodile skin'—made trainee scribes laugh for centuries.

story_check.question: According to the final line of Kheti's poem, what made a scribe's job different from every other trade?
options: Scribes never had to learn how to count
Scribes worked outdoors in muddy fields
Every other job had a boss, whereas the scribe gave the orders
Scribes wore heavy bronze armour all summer
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Dua-Kheti teased that every other job had a boss, while respected scribes counted taxes, kept royal records, and gave out orders.

monday_cold_call.question: In the Ancient Egyptian poem 'The Satire of the Trades', how did father Dua-Kheti persuade his son Pepi to work hard at scribe school?
monday_cold_call.answer: He joked about the aching arms, mosquitoes, wet clay, and lurking crocodiles in other jobs, reminding Pepi that scribes gave out the orders.

hinge_question: Can historians trust 'The Satire of the Trades' to tell the whole truth about Egyptian craftworkers, once we spot who wrote it and why?

book_title: One Feather Against a Lifetime: Scribe Ani's Book of the Dead
author: The History Revision Hub Narrative Archive
provenance_note: Original historical narrative grounded in the real 19th-Dynasty 'Papyrus of Ani' (c. 1250 BC, Thebes; British Museum EA10470), including the authentic Egyptian heart-scarab plea from Spell 30B.
author_context: Around 1250 BC in Thebes, a real royal scribe named Ani paid master artists to paint a twenty-four-metre papyrus scroll for his tomb. Step inside the scene painted on that scroll as Ani faces the golden scales!
cover_caption: Ancient Egyptian bronze statuette decorated with gold leaf, showing jackal-headed god Anubis standing before a kneeling worshipper.

vocabVault.def: The jackal-headed Egyptian god of embalming and tombs who checked the golden scales in the underworld.
The Egyptian goddess of truth, fairness, and cosmic balance, represented by a single light ostrich feather.
The fearsome underworld monster—part crocodile, lion, and hippopotamus—waiting to gobble up heavy, selfish hearts.
Ancient Egypt's sunny afterlife paradise of green canals and rich harvests ruled by green-skinned Osiris.

extract: Around 1250 BC in Thebes, artists painted a long papyrus scroll in blue, red, and gold for a real scribe named Ani. Rolled inside Ani's tomb, this Book of the Dead showed the toughest afterlife test in the Hall of Two Truths. In the scene, Ani bows in clean white linen beside his wife Tutu while forty-two gods watch from above. Kneeling before tall golden scales, jackal-headed Anubis steadies the brass pointer. On one pan sits Ani's heart. Priests left it inside his mummy chest because Egyptians believed the heart kept every good and bad memory. On the other pan rests one light white feather from Ma'at, goddess of truth. Right below crouches Ammit the Devourer, snapping crocodile jaws on a lion-and-hippo body! Holding his breath, Ani whispers his plea. "O my heart, do not stand as a witness against me!" Ibis-headed Thoth marks his tablet. The pans stay level, and Osiris welcomes kind Ani into the sunny Field of Reeds.

parent_discussion.question: Why did priests leave Ani's heart inside his mummy chest instead of taking it out?
parent_discussion.answer: Egyptians believed the heart kept every good and bad memory from a person's life, so Anubis needed to weigh it on the golden scales.

parent_discussion.question: Why was an ostrich feather the perfect symbol to place on the opposite pan of the scales?
parent_discussion.answer: A single feather is almost weightless, showing that a person's heart had to be completely free of heavy lies, cruelty, and greed.

parent_discussion.question: Ani whispered, 'O my heart, do not stand as a witness against me!' What does this afterlife test tell us about what Ancient Egyptians thought made a good person?
parent_discussion.answer: It shows that kindness, truth, and fairness mattered most—only a light, honest heart could balance Ma'at's feather and reach the sunny Field of Reeds.

story_check.question: Who checked the pointer on the golden scales during Scribe Ani's judgement?
options: Jackal-headed god Anubis
Greek god Poseidon
King Narmer of Upper Egypt
Scribe Dua-Kheti
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Jackal-headed Anubis knelt right beside the balance beam while ibis-headed Thoth recorded the result.

story_check.question: Which three fierce animals combined to form Ammit the Devourer waiting beneath the scales?
options: Eagle, cobra, and bull
Crocodile, lion, and hippopotamus
Wolf, scorpion, and vulture
Shark, leopard, and camel
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Crocodile, lion, and hippo were the three deadliest animals known along Egypt's Nile valley.

story_check.question: What happened when Ani's heart balanced lightly with Ma'at's feather of truth?
options: Ammit swallowed his heart at once
He was sent back to scribe school
Osiris welcomed him into the peaceful Field of Reeds
His tomb was opened to desert sandstorms
story_check.feedback: Well done! A light, truthful heart earned eternal life in Osiris's green Field of Reeds.

monday_cold_call.question: On Scribe Ani's 'Book of the Dead' scroll, what was weighed against his heart, and what happened if a heart was heavy with cruel deeds?
monday_cold_call.answer: Ma'at's feather of truth was weighed against the heart; if heavy with bad deeds, Ammit (crocodile, lion, and hippo) gobbled it up.

hinge_question: Why did Egyptians tuck a stone scarab charm whispering 'Do not stand as a witness against me!' right over a mummy's heart?

book_title: Pharaoh Hatshepsut's Karnak Obelisk & Punt Inscriptions
author: Pharaoh Hatshepsut (Carved at Thebes, c. 1460 BC)
provenance_note: Age-calibrated primary translation adapted directly from Pharaoh Hatshepsut's first-person hieroglyphic inscriptions on her red-granite Karnak obelisk base and the Punt Colonnade at Deir el-Bahari (trans. James Henry Breasted, 1906, Public Domain).
author_context: Around 1479 BC, royal woman Hatshepsut crowned herself full Pharaoh of Egypt, complete with the striped royal headcloth and ceremonial false beard! Read the proud message she carved into stone for people living thousands of years after her.
cover_caption: View looking down from the desert cliffs at Deir el-Bahari onto the sweeping stone ramps and pillared terraces of Pharaoh Hatshepsut's temple.

vocabVault.def: One of Ancient Egypt's most successful female pharaohs, famous for peaceful sea trade and grand stone temples.
A tall, four-sided stone pillar tapering to a pointed pyramid tip, carved from a single block of red granite.
A distant trading land south along the Red Sea coast, rich in gold, ebony wood, and sweet frankincense trees.
Hatshepsut's breathtaking terraced cliff temple near Thebes where carvers pictured her ships sailing to Punt.

extract: Around 1460 BC, female Pharaoh Hatshepsut had stonemasons carve her own proud words onto tall granite obelisks at Karnak. More carvings lined her bright cliff temple at Deir el-Bahari. Speaking across the ages, she addressed everyone who would ever stand below her stones. "Listen closely, all you people yet unborn who shall see this monument in future years! Do not say, 'I do not know why this was made.' Truly, I sat quiet inside my palace and remembered great Amun who shaped me. My heart led me to raise two tall red granite obelisks from Aswan. Their gleaming gold tips shine across both banks of the Nile!" "I also sent five great wooden ships south down the Red Sea to the Land of Punt. No ruler before me brought back living frankincense trees with baskets of earth round their roots! Now sweet smoke fills Karnak's halls, and my name shall live forever in stone."

parent_discussion.question: Who was Pharaoh Hatshepsut speaking to when she carved 'all you people yet unborn' onto her tall granite obelisks?
parent_discussion.answer: She was speaking directly to future people standing below her stones centuries later—including us reading her words today!

parent_discussion.question: Why was Hatshepsut so proud of bringing back living frankincense trees with baskets of earth round their roots?
parent_discussion.answer: Because no ruler before her had brought back whole living trees to plant in Egypt, so their sweet incense smoke could fill Karnak's halls year after year.

parent_discussion.question: Hatshepsut wanted her name to 'live forever in stone'—what achievements did she choose to be remembered for instead of fighting wars?
parent_discussion.answer: She chose to be remembered for peaceful sea trade to the Land of Punt, raising gleaming gold-tipped red granite obelisks at Karnak, and building her grand cliff temple at Deir el-Bahari.

story_check.question: What shone on the pointed tops of Hatshepsut's red granite obelisks at Karnak?
options: Painted wooden flags
Gleaming gold caps catching sunlight across both banks of the Nile
Iron beacons burning coal
Blue glass hippo statues
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Shining precious metal caps caught the morning sun first so worshippers miles away saw Amun's temple gleam.

story_check.question: How many ships did Hatshepsut send south down the Red Sea to the Land of Punt?
options: One tiny reed canoe
Five great wooden sailing ships
Two hundred bronze triremes
Fifty camel caravans
story_check.feedback: Correct! Five large sailing ships carried Egyptian gifts south and returned laden with Punt's treasures.

story_check.question: What rare living cargo did Hatshepsut's sailors carry home in baskets of earth?
options: Living frankincense trees for temple gardens
Snowy pine trees from Greece
Mesoamerican cacao bushes
Prickly desert cacti
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Her sailors carried living frankincense trees with baskets of earth round their roots so sweet incense could fill Karnak's halls.

monday_cold_call.question: What two achievements did female Pharaoh Hatshepsut boast about to 'all you people yet unborn' on her obelisks and cliff temple?
monday_cold_call.answer: Raising two gold-tipped red granite obelisks at Karnak and sending five wooden ships to the Land of Punt to bring back living frankincense trees.

hinge_question: Why did female Pharaoh Hatshepsut ask sculptors to carve her wearing the traditional striped headcloth and false beard of a king?

book_title: Sixteen Buried Steps: Uncovering Tutankhamun's Tomb
author: The History Revision Hub Narrative Archive
provenance_note: Original historical micro-story grounded in Howard Carter's November 1922 excavation journal in the Griffith Institute (Oxford) and documented accounts of Egyptian water-boy Hussein Abdel Rassoul uncovering the top step of KV62.
author_context: For years, experts insisted nothing remained left to find in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Discover how a young Egyptian water-boy's digging stick in November 1922 led to the most dazzling archaeological moment in history!
cover_caption: Gilded backrest of Tutankhamun's throne from tomb KV62, showing Queen Ankhesenamun touching the young pharaoh's shoulder beneath golden sunbeams.

vocabVault.def: The New Kingdom boy-pharaoh crowned aged nine around 1332 BC whose hidden cliff tomb escaped ancient grave robbers.
A hot, secret desert canyon opposite Thebes where New Kingdom pharaohs cut deep rock tombs underground.
Carefully digging, brushing, photographing, and recording buried historical objects without damaging clues.
A heavy carved stone coffin holding royal nested coffins and Tutankhamun's eleven-kilogram solid gold mask.

extract: On 4 November 1922, fierce sun baked the rocky floor in Egypt's Valley of the Kings. Near old stone huts, young water-boy Hussein Abdel Rassoul scooped away loose sand for heavy clay water jars. Suddenly, his stick struck flat, cut rock! Egyptian diggers brushed away gravel and found sixteen steep stone steps going down into the cliff. At the foot stood a plastered door stamped with royal jackal seals three thousand years old! British archaeologist Howard Carter wired his backer, Lord Carnarvon, to sail out from England at once. On 26 November, Carter chipped a small hole in the inner door and held a lit candle inside. Warm ancient air rushed out and made the tiny flame dance wildly. Slowly, gold couches, statues, chariots, and a shining throne glinted through the gloom! Behind him, Carnarvon whispered tensely. "Can you see anything?" Carter breathed back in awe. "Yes, wonderful things!"

parent_discussion.question: How did young water-boy Hussein Abdel Rassoul accidentally uncover the hidden stone steps on 4 November 1922?
parent_discussion.answer: He was using his stick to scoop away loose sand for heavy clay water jars near old stone huts when he suddenly struck flat, cut rock.

parent_discussion.question: Why did Howard Carter wait from 4 November until 26 November before chipping a tiny hole in the inner door?
parent_discussion.answer: He waited for his backer Lord Carnarvon to sail all the way out from England, and he opened the door carefully so no buried clues or treasures were damaged.

parent_discussion.question: Imagine standing right behind Howard Carter in the dark tunnel as his candle flame danced—what must it have felt like to hear him whisper, 'Yes, wonderful things!'?
parent_discussion.answer: It would have felt breathless and magical, as gold couches, statues, chariots, and a shining throne slowly glinted out of a tomb sealed for three thousand years.

story_check.question: Who uncovered the very first buried stone step of Tutankhamun's tomb in November 1922?
options: French scholar Jean-François Champollion
Young Egyptian water-boy Hussein Abdel Rassoul
Greek general Alexander the Great
Queen Cleopatra VII
story_check.feedback: Spot on! Hussein Abdel Rassoul struck the top cut stone step while scooping sand for heavy clay water jars.

story_check.question: Why did the candle flame flicker wildly when Howard Carter poked it through the small hole in the door?
options: A desert thunderstorm was blowing snow inside
Warm three-thousand-year-old air rushed out through the opening
River Nile water was flooding the steps
Bats knocked the candle out of his hand
story_check.feedback: Exactly right! Escaping air from the sealed chamber made the flame dance before the gold glinted in the light.

story_check.question: What famous words did Howard Carter reply when Lord Carnarvon asked, 'Can you see anything?'
options: 'Only empty dust and broken pots!'
'Yes, wonderful things!'
'Quick, fetch the dynamite!'
'Somebody already took the throne!'
story_check.feedback: Iconic! As his eyes adjusted to the candlelight, gold couches, statues, chariots, and a shining throne glinted through the gloom.

monday_cold_call.question: How did young water-boy Hussein Abdel Rassoul find the hidden steps of Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922, and what did Howard Carter whisper when he peered inside?
monday_cold_call.answer: Hussein struck flat, cut rock with his stick while scooping sand for clay water jars, and Carter whispered, 'Yes, wonderful things!' as gold treasures gleamed by candlelight.

hinge_question: If Tutankhamun died aged just nineteen as a minor ruler, why is he more famous today than pharaohs who ruled Egypt for sixty years?
